newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters calls NZ markets fiscal view overoptimistic.
newsitem.headline: Peters calls NZ markets fiscal view overoptimistic.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, speaking after giving a speech to a business lunch meeting, said he felt market observers had too optimistic a view of the country's fiscal prospects ahead of next week's budget.
Asked if financial markets had been too complacent about the fiscal outlook, Peters told Reuters, "No, I think they have been considerably too optimistic".

Asked to comment on speculation that the government's 1997/98 surplus forecast to be released next week might have fallen to around NZ$ 2.0 billion, Peters told reporters, "You know I can't confirm or deny any of those things."
In his speech, he had said that a combination of structural and one-off factors meant projected surpluses would be lower, "particularly in 1997/98", than some recent forecasts.
Several of these have centred around $NZ2.9 billion.
"What I was doing was asking people to moderate their calculations, have regard for the information that is not public and to factor these things in," he explained afterwards.
Peters, who has been critical of recent business confidence surveys which have shown a lot of negative sentiment about the economy, stuck to his line that conditions are not so bad.

Asked what he thought the lower fiscal projections would do for business confidence, he said, "I think business have really got to snap out of that. All the fundamentals are correct and good. We have got the kind of environment that other countries would envy".
Asked what he thought about the concerns expressed by some business people he said, "It's a state of mind.

"If they think about it seriously ... if they think of all the things that could have changed that did not, in terms of political stability... they have all the cause in the world to be optimistic," Peters said.
The budget, he said, would "have a human face" and form an environment in which business could prosper.
